For $p = 2$: $(2+1)k - 1 = 3k - 1$

For $p = 5$: $(5+1)k - 1 = 6k - 1$
For $p = 7$: $(7+1)k - 1 = 8k - 1$
For $p = 11$: $(11+1)k - 1 = 12k - 1$

So we need $3k-1, 4k-1, 6k-1, 8k-1, 12k-1, \ldots$ all to be composite.

Let me think about this differently. We want $(p+1)k \equiv 1 \pmod{q}$ for some prime $q$ that divides $(p+1)k - 1$, where $q < (p+1)k - 1$ (so it's composite, not equal to $q$).

By Chinese Remainder Theorem, if we can cover all primes $p$ with congruences on $k$ modulo various $q_i$, and these congruences are compatible, then we can find such $k$.

The congruence $(p+1)k \equiv 1 \pmod{q}$ means $k \equiv (p+1)^{-1} \pmod{q}$, which requires $\gcd(p+1, q) = 1$, i.e., $q \nmid p+1$.

So for each prime $p$, we pick a prime $q$ with $q \nmid (p+1)$, and set $k \equiv (p+1)^{-1} \pmod{q}$.

The challenge: we need to cover ALL primes $p$ with finitely many congruence conditions on $k$, and these conditions must be compatible (CRT).
